paper_name: A Scheduling Algorithm to Reduce the Static Energy Consumption of Multiprocessor Real-Time Systems
paper_description: This paper proposes an offline scheduling algorithm (LPDPM) for multiprocessor real-time systems that minimizes static energy consumption by maximizing idle periods. It uses mixed-integer linear programming to generate an optimal schedule offline and an online scheduler to handle task execution and dynamic slack time. The core schedulability contribution lies in the formal proof of optimality for a specific scheduling algorithm used online.

formal_description.statement: The weight of an idle task τ in an interval k, denoted by b_k + e_k, can be split into two subtasks, b_k executed at the beginning of the interval and e_k at the end, without increasing energy consumption. These two subtasks of τ can never be preempted.

variables.b_k: weight of the beginning subtask of idle task τ in interval k
variables.e_k: weight of the ending subtask of idle task τ in interval k
variables.τ: idle task representing expected idle time

assumptions: The idle task τ is split into two subtasks, τ_b and τ_e.
τ_b is executed at the beginning of an interval, and τ_e at the end.
The total weight of τ in interval k is b_k + e_k.
formal_description.conclusion: The splitting of the idle task into two non-preemptible subtasks executed at the boundaries of intervals is valid for energy minimization and does not negatively impact schedulability.

informal_sketch.intuition: By splitting the 'idle time' task into two parts, one at the start and one at the end of an interval, we can better manage how idle periods merge and extend. Crucially, these 'idle time' parts are designed to be non-preemptible to ensure they can be used to extend idle periods without being interrupted by other tasks.
steps: Consider an interval k. The total 'idle time' required in this interval is represented by the weight b_k + e_k.
We propose to execute a portion b_k at the very beginning of interval k and another portion e_k at the very end of interval k.
This strategy does not reduce the total 'idle time' available within the interval, thus not negatively impacting schedulability.

Furthermore, by assigning the highest priority to the beginning subtask (τ_b) and the lowest to the ending subtask (τ_e), we ensure they are executed at their designated times. The proof for non-preemption relies on the fact that if τ_b were to be preempted, it would imply all other processors are busy with tasks that also have zero laxity, which contradicts the assumption that τ_b still needs to execute. Similarly, τ_e, having the lowest laxity, will only be scheduled when its laxity becomes zero, meaning it won't be preempted during its execution.
informal_sketch.pseudocode: Assign highest priority to τ_b and lowest priority to τ_e. Schedule τ_b at the start of interval k. Schedule τ_e at the end of interval k. Ensure no other task preempts τ_b or τ_e during their execution.
key_insights: Splitting the idle task allows for better control over idle period merging.
Non-preemptibility of idle task subtasks is crucial for their role in extending idle periods.

formal_description.statement: FPZL is optimal for implicit-deadline tasks sharing a common period.

variables.FPZL: Fixed Priority until Zero Laxity scheduling algorithm
variables.laxity: remaining time in the interval - remaining execution time of a job in the interval

assumptions: All tasks share a common period (or are within a common interval).
The scheduler monitors pending jobs and schedules them when their laxity becomes zero.
formal_description.conclusion: If a task misses its deadline under FPZL, it implies a contradiction with the system's utilization, proving that FPZL will always meet all deadlines under these conditions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem states that if we have a set of tasks that all need to finish by the same deadline (the end of an interval), and we use a priority-based scheduler that always runs the task with the least 'wiggle room' (zero laxity), then we are guaranteed to meet all deadlines. The proof works by contradiction: if a deadline is missed, it means the scheduler couldn't make room for a task that was about to miss its deadline, which implies the system was overloaded to begin with.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that a task τ misses its deadline at the end of an interval.
If τ misses its deadline, it means that at some point, its laxity became negative, or it was not scheduled when its laxity was zero.
If τ was not scheduled when its laxity was zero, it implies that all other m processors were busy executing tasks that also had zero laxity and could not be preempted.

If all m processors are busy with tasks that have zero laxity and cannot be preempted, and τ still has remaining execution time, it means the total required execution time for all tasks in that interval exceeds the available processing time (m processors).
This scenario (total utilization > m) contradicts the initial assumption that the task set is schedulable within the interval (i.e., global utilization is no more than m).
Therefore, the initial assumption that a deadline miss can occur must be false, proving that FPZL is optimal for tasks sharing a common period.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
1. For each interval, assign static priorities to tasks.
2. Monitor the laxity of all pending jobs.
3. At any point in time, schedule the m jobs with the lowest laxity on the m processors.
4. If a job's laxity reaches zero, ensure it is scheduled, preempting lower-priority jobs if necessary.
5. If a job misses its deadline, a contradiction is reached.
key_insights: The concept of 'laxity' is key to determining urgency.
The proof by contradiction effectively shows that an overloaded system is the only cause for a deadline miss under FPZL.
This theorem is crucial for the online scheduler's ability to manage tasks within intervals.
